added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: with an ETF, you have an NAV that fluctuates during the day because you know what the underlying portfolio looks like and that changes your pricing
added_claims.claim: Unlike a mutual fund (one end-of-day NAV), an ETF has an intraday NAV but trades at market prices set by bids and offers, and market makers who profit from order-book imbalance keep the price near NAV, though sometimes better and sometimes worse.
added_claims.indicator: ETF price versus intraday NAV, bid-ask spread
added_claims.conditions: depth of market makers and liquidity of the underlying
added_claims.testable: yes - premium or discount to NAV and spread data

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: they're often incredibly focused on the one or two three things that can go wrong and make them look bad
added_claims.claim: Financial advisors fear visible, avoidable mistakes (for example a market order that moves an ETF price by 50 bp), so an ETF must trade tightly to NAV to be adopted by advisors who grew up with mutual funds.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: There are other allocators who want to build those building blocks themselves.
added_claims.claim: Allocators split into two groups: those who want a one-stop multi-strategy ETF that fills the alternatives bucket with an absolute-return profile, and those who want to assemble the building blocks themselves, which sets the product design.

added_claims.speaker: Eric Crittenden
added_claims.quote: They're staring at that line item risk. They're staring at the the statement risk.
added_claims.claim: Even after agreeing with the math, a standalone managed-futures holding creates a visible line item whose every monthly move triggers questions from clients, regulators and compliance; this micromanagement is a main reason allocators abandon it.
added_claims.testable: partly - holding periods of allocators in standalone managed futures versus blended products

added_claims.speaker: Eric Crittenden
added_claims.quote: if I can build a good managed features program and don't charge hedge fund fees, you know, don't charge the 2 and 20, uh, and have something that's scalable
added_claims.claim: A managed-futures product built without hedge-fund fees, scalable, and combined with low-fee tax-efficient equity exposure solves the product-market fit problem and a set-and-forget holding that the manager would use with his own money.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: there is no addressable market. There are hundreds of submarkets out there.
added_claims.claim: The alternatives market is not one pool but hundreds of submarkets with different needs, so a product succeeds by choosing one specific allocator segment (for example ETF model allocators who need a 3-5% diversifier) instead of trying to serve everyone.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: to me JP Morgan is doing something like very very serious and credible. They're going to a team who knows how to do this.
added_claims.claim: Large-firm trend products are credible when built by experienced trend teams (JP Morgan's quant team, Fidelity's hire of Rob Crochet) rather than by generalists given an engineering degree, which is the diligence test between serious and opportunistic entrants.

corrections.issue: Speaker mix-up and merge: the remarks that the index drags in the biggest managers' blowups and omits smaller managers are Niels's, but the point that big institutions do not pay the fees embedded in the SG CTA index (and that the trend index has a slightly higher Sharpe) is made by Andrew Beer, not Niels.
corrections.fix: Niels: CTA indices contain the biggest managers and their blowups and omit smaller managers who do well, so they may not reflect the industry at its best. Beer: large institutions do not pay the fees built into the SG CTA index, so index Sharpe ratios do not describe what they earn.

corrections.issue: Recorded as the speaker stated it, but the arithmetic does not hold under simple diversification: two uncorrelated strategies with Sharpe 0.4 at equal risk combine to about 0.57, and reaching 1.1 needs a correlation near -0.7. Treat the 1.1-1.2 figure as the speaker's unverified rule of thumb, and note he says himself that it may not be sustainable.
corrections.fix: Eric Crittenden says that combining roughly 0.4-Sharpe strategies (equities, managed futures) gets a Sharpe near 1.1, and adding about 0.3 from tail-risk hedging and another strategy gets near 1.2; this is the speaker's claim and is not supported by simple arithmetic unless the strategies are strongly negatively correlated.

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - first reader captured the core trend, simplicity, Sharpe and behavioral arguments well; missed ETF mechanics detail, June 2026 monthly performance, index composition and ranking evidence, allocator segmentation and several product-design remarks.
